title: Boss: follow the packet
summary: Three networking tickets on a real Kubernetes cluster: refused connections, a look inside with port-forward, and a broken chain across namespaces.

steps.title: The scene
body: Networking tickets, each on its own one-node **Kubernetes 1.37** cluster. Work along the path a request takes: the
name (DNS), the Service (selector, ports, endpoints), the policy, the pod. Use `kubectl get endpointslices`,
`kubectl describe svc`, `kubectl exec ... wget`, `kubectl port-forward` and `kubectl get networkpolicy`.

steps.title: Ticket 1: "connection refused" through the Service
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `orders` runs two healthy pods, and the Service `orders` even lists them as endpoints, yet
`kubectl exec shell -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://orders/` gets `Connection refused`. Fix it without touching the

checks.name: a request through the Service answers
checks.cmd: timeout 20 sh -c 'until kubectl exec shell -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://orders/ 2>/dev/null | grep -q "^Name:"; do sleep 1; done' ; kubectl exec shell -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://orders/ | grep '^Name:'

checks.name: the endpoints are on the app's port
checks.cmd: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders -n default -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | .ports[0].port as $p | .endpoints[]? | select(.conditions.ready) | $p] | "\(length) ready on \(.[0])"'
checks.fail: The Service's `targetPort` should be the port the container listens on.

hints: Endpoints exist, so the selector is right. Compare the endpoint port with the container's port.
`kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders -o wide` and `kubectl get deploy orders -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].ports}'`.
steps.explain: "No endpoints" and "connection refused" are different failures: the first is the selector, the second is the port. kube-proxy forwards to `podIP:targetPort` whether or not anything listens there, so the Service looks fine while every connection is refused. Referring to a **named** container port makes the mapping survive a port change in the Deployment.

steps.title: Ticket 2: look at an internal service from your machine
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The `ledger` Service in the namespace `payments` has no external exposure, and must not get one.
You need to look at it from **this machine** (as you would from your laptop).
1. Use `kubectl port-forward` to make the Service reachable on `localhost:8081` (run it in the background with `&`).
2. Request `http://localhost:8081/` and write the value of the `Hostname:` line it returns (the pod that answered)
3. Leave the Service as it is: still `ClusterIP`.

checks.name: pod.txt names the ledger pod
checks.fail: Not the pod that answered. `curl -s localhost:8081/ | grep Hostname`.

checks.name: ledger is still a ClusterIP Service
checks.cmd: kubectl -n payments get svc ledger -o jsonpath='{.spec.type}'
checks.fail: Leave the Service as `ClusterIP`: port-forward needs no exposure.

hints: `kubectl port-forward -n payments svc/ledger 8081:80 &` forwards local 8081 to the Service's port 80 (one of its pods).
`curl -s localhost:8081/ | sed -n 's/^Hostname: //p' > ~/answers/pod.txt`, then `kill %1` to stop the forward.
steps.explain: `kubectl port-forward` tunnels through the API server to one pod (picked from the Service), so you can reach an internal service without a LoadBalancer, NodePort or Gateway, and without changing anything. It is the everyday way to open a database or an admin page from a laptop; it needs `pods/portforward` permission, which is why RBAC grants it carefully.

steps.title: Ticket 3: checkout cannot reach inventory
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `checkout` (namespace `shop`) calls `inventory` (namespace `stock`) and logs an error every few
seconds: `kubectl -n shop logs deploy/checkout --tail=2`. Three things are wrong along the path. Fix them so its newest
log line says `inventory OK`, keeping the network policy in place (it should let `checkout` in, alongside the old

checks.name: checkout reaches inventory
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop rollout status deploy/checkout --timeout=30s >/dev/null && sleep 4 && kubectl -n shop logs $(kubectl -n shop get pods -l app=checkout -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .metadata.name') --tail=1
checks.fail: `checkout`'s newest log line does not say `inventory OK`. Work along the path: name, Service, policy.

checks.name: the Service has endpoints
checks.cmd: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=inventory -n stock -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | .ports[0].port as $p | .endpoints[]? | select(.conditions.ready) | $p] | "\(length) ready on \(.[0])"'

checks.name: a policy still guards inventory
checks.cmd: kubectl -n stock get networkpolicy -o name | grep -c .
checks.fail: Keep a NetworkPolicy on `inventory`: allow `checkout`, do not delete the guard.

checks.name: other pods in shop are still kept out
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop run probe --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never --rm -i --command -- sh -c 'wget -qO- -T 2 http://inventory.stock/ >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo reached || echo blocked' 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'reached|blocked'
checks.fail: Any pod in `shop` can reach inventory now: allow `app=checkout` only.

hints: The URL names the namespace `shop`, but the Service lives in `stock`.
`kubectl -n stock get endpointslices` is empty: the Service's selector asks for a label the pods do not have. The policy only lets `app=frontend` in.

`kubectl -n shop set env deploy/checkout INVENTORY_URL=http://inventory.stock.svc.cluster.local/`, `kubectl -n stock patch svc inventory --type=json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/selector/tier"}]'`, and add `app=checkout` to the policy's `from`.
solution: kubectl -n stock get networkpolicy inventory-ingress -o yaml
steps.explain: Every hop fails differently: a wrong namespace in the name gives `bad address`, a selector mismatch gives a Service with no endpoints (timeouts), and a policy drops packets silently (timeouts too). Checking in path order (name, endpoints, policy) finds all three instead of guessing. A `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` in the **same** `from` entry mean AND; as separate entries they would mean OR, a classic policy mistake.
